<reason>A very close, high-quality exchange. PRO (B) built a compelling normative frame (honest pricing, fairness, business-owned costs), neutralized the Meyer example as a coordination failure, and landed "one boss plus table nine" against CON's manager-leverage point. But CON (A) steadily narrowed the debate to the question of whether servers actually end up with more money, and PRO progressively conceded ground: "the honest number is smaller" for winners, then the muddled closing line "honest prices are smaller than dishonest ones," which A exploited cleanly as "the motion promises a raise and delivers a pay cut." A's full-minimum-plus-tips states point (servers keep tips even without a tip credit) was never squarely answered, and the "$9-check diner can only pay what it can afford" mechanism undercut PRO's unsupported assertion that the median gains. A's costs: two clipped turns, and a misdescription of PRO as having "owned" the median pay cut. Those keep the margin thin, but A left the reader with the sharper reason to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2/Closing turn on PRO's own concession: after PRO admitted the $30/hour server takes a cut and that the pass-through is "smaller," A reframed the whole motion as "a pay cut you can see in advance is still a pay cut," directly against a proposition promising higher pay—the most decisive unanswered move in the debate.</best_rebuttal>
